fixes.explanation: Verse 9 says, "The fear of the LORD is pure, enduring forever…" Forever, friend. Everything else in my kitchen wears out eventually, even my best mixing bowl. David says this one doesn't, because it endures forever.

Verse 3 says it plainly: "Without speech or language, without a sound to be heard…" So the sky speaks, and you can't hear a thing. Friend, that's the quietest sermon ever preached, and its voice still goes out into all the earth (Psalm 19:4).

Kingdom is a fair guess, but it isn't David's word. He says the voice has gone out into all the earth, with words reaching "…the ends of the world." No borders, no passports. The sky doesn't stop at any kingdom's edge.
It's actually true. David says the sun is "Like a bridegroom emerging from his chamber…" in verse 5. Right after that comes a second picture of the sun, a champion. So the answer is True, friend.

A king? Bowing? Not in this verse, friend. The champion is "…rejoicing to run his course…" He's not bowing to anybody, he's too busy being glad about the run! That's the picture David uses for the sun taking off across the sky.

Verse 8 says, "the commandments of the LORD are radiant, giving light to the eyes." Radiant and giving light, friend. It's like somebody finally flipped the switch in a dark room. I spent years in the back of a dark junk drawer, so believe me, light matters.
That's right, friend. David says, "the judgments of the LORD are true, being altogether righteous." Altogether! That word doesn't leave a single crumb of "partly" on the counter.

Yes, friend. Verse 11 says, "By them indeed Your servant is warned; in keeping them is great reward." David says the LORD's words warn him, and that great reward is found in keeping them. That's worth knowing in any kitchen.

It's actually true. David says, "in keeping them is great reward." Right before that, he says that by them "…Your servant is warned…" So the warning comes through the LORD's words, and the great reward is in keeping them.

David asks, "Cleanse me from my hidden faults." He just asked, "Who can discern his own errors?" so he asks God to cleanse the faults he may not even see. That's an honest prayer, friend. I think it's a good one to borrow.
The psalm ends with "…O LORD, my Rock and my Redeemer." Two names, and David finishes his whole prayer on them. I think that's a strong place to land, friend.

Shepherd and King are fine names, friend, but David doesn't use them in this line. He closes with "…O LORD, my Rock and my Redeemer." That comes right after he asks that the words of his mouth and the meditation of his heart be pleasing in God's sight. So no shepherd and no crown here, just a Rock and a Redeemer.

Light and shield sound like a strong team, friend, but David doesn't use them here. He ends with "…O LORD, my Rock and my Redeemer." Those are the last two names he gives the LORD in the whole psalm. He lets them be the final word.
